notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0040.stoa036b.opp-l: Scanning errors silently corrected throughout (e.g. 'Praebete sileo.. tinm' = 'Praebete silentium', 'sunum' = 'sanum', 'Evange- Hi' = 'Evangelii'). Ch. 3: 'quam dum tempus' is awkward; rendered as if 'quam tempus'. Ch. 5 heading: 'hi die judicii' read as 'in die judicii'. 'Oriens' (Luke 1:78) rendered 'the Rising', playing on 'occasus' (setting). Scripture references follow the edition's numbering (Vulgate psalm numbering; 4 Kings = 2 Kings).

Scanning errors corrected silently where evident (e.g. 'raro' for 'caro', 'rupimus' for 'cupimus', 'mortis tinctus' read as 'mortis timemus', 'noli poterit' for 'non poterit'). In VII 'errorum calliculi' is uncertain; rendered as 'little paths of error' (diminutive of callis). In X 'conspersum' taken as 'dough', continuing the leaven image. Square-bracketed clauses in X are as marked by the edition.

Line 13: the chapter summary's 'Tristitia sulutaris quwnnm' is read as 'Tristitia salutaris quaenam'. 'commea.us vitae' read as 'commeatus vitae' (extension/respite of life). 'pepercerint vestimento' presumably means not tearing their clothes in mourning. Line 14: 'Hic Incus cultor' is taken as 'hic lucus cultor' ('this worshipper of groves'); the reading is uncertain. The unnamed pagan ruler (marked with an editorial note '(a)') is not identified in the text; the story is told in Roman sources of Horatius Pulvillus at the dedication of the Capitol, but this cannot be confirmed from the passage. 'Hortabamur lilios' read as 'hortabatur filios'.

Line 16: 'mortis communis' lacks a noun (perhaps 'lege' or 'conditione'); '[the law]' is supplied. 'Lippes' read as 'lippitudines' (bleariness). In the Admonitio, 'vetulas' refers to the pagan New Year masquerade ('making the old woman'); the gloss 'little old women' keeps the edition's reading against Sirmond's 'vitulas'. 'Germanensis' = the Saint-Germain manuscript.

nodes.text: ON THE CONSOLATION OF THE DEAD
First sermon.

CHAPTER ONE. Sorrow is twofold. Give [me your] silence, brothers, so that a sermon that is useful and necessary at this time may not pass you by. For medicine is needed most of all when a serious illness arises; and an eye-salve must be applied with care when the eye has been troubled by pain. So whoever does not have this pain should not make a noise, but rather listen; for it does no harm to a healthy man to know a medicine that is beneficial. But whoever, through this misfortune, has the eye of the mind troubled and is tormented by pains, let him be all the more attentive to open his eye to receive the eye-salve of the saving word, by which he may obtain not only consolation but also a remedy. Now it is certain that one who has a painful eye, if he refuses to open it when the physician is pouring in the salve, the salve is poured outside, beyond the pupil, while the eye remains in pain. So too the mind of one who grieves, if through excessive sorrow it shuts itself against the word, and does not receive the healthful admonition, will begin to grieve more, and perhaps suffer what is contained in Scripture, That the sorrow of the world works death (2 Cor. 7:10). The blessed apostle Paul, teacher of the faithful and saving physician, said that there are two sorrows, one good and the other bad; one useful and the other useless; one that saves and the other that destroys. And so that what I say may not seem doubtful to anyone, I will recite his very words. For he says, The sorrow that is according to God works repentance unto a steadfast salvation: this is the good sorrow. Then follows, For the sorrow of this world works death (ibid.): this is the bad one.

CHAPTER II. The causes of mourning for the dead, with respect to the dead themselves, are shown to be vain. Let us see then, brothers, whether this sorrow which is now at hand, which is now at work in the breast and is heard in the voice, is useful or useless; whether it can help or harm. See, the lifeless body lies there; there lies on the bier a man without the man, limbs indeed without spirit: he is called aloud, and does not answer; he is summoned, and does not hear; the face lies pale, the form changed, through which death itself is seen. Besides, one thinks of his perpetual silence, one thinks of the delight [he gave], either that which was or the benefit that was to come; one thinks of needs [he met]; his sweetest words come to mind; a long familiarity is missed. These without doubt are what move tears, incite wailing, and sink the whole soul into deep sorrow. Against these weapons of grief, so powerful, so strong, this must first of all be set: that everything born in this world must die. For this is the law of God and the unchangeable sentence which the first of the human race received after his sin, when God said, Earth you are, and into earth you shall go (Gen. 3:19). What new thing then has happened, if a man born for this has satisfied the divine law and sentence? What new thing has occurred, if one born of mortals has answered to his own nature, since he could not excuse himself from it? What is ancient is not unusual; what is daily is not unheard of; what is common is not peculiar [to one]. If we know that our grandfathers and great-grandfathers set out by this road of death, if finally we have heard that the Patriarchs and Prophets themselves, from Adam the first-formed, did not depart from the world without passing away, let us raise our soul from the depth of sorrow: for he has paid what he owed. And surely, when a debt is paid, what sorrow can it hold? This is truly a debt which no money can redeem; this is a debt from which neither strength nor wisdom nor power excuses, and which not even kings themselves will be able to avoid. Plainly I would urge you to increase your sorrow, if it had been the kind of thing which, though it could have been redeemed or put off by your wealth, had come about through negligence or stinginess. But since the decree of God is firm and unchangeable, we grieve in vain and ask of ourselves why he died, since it is written, To the Lord God belong the issues of death (Ps. 67:21). If then this common condition of life is taken into the mind, the burdened eye of the heart will begin to be relieved, as if by the first application [of the salve].

CHAPTER III. Other [causes], with respect to ourselves, are no more reasonable. Why excessive sorrow works death. But you say, I know this misfortune is common, I know that he who has died has paid his debt; but I think of the delight, I recall the needs [he met], I miss the familiarity. If you are affected by sorrow on account of these, you are led by error, not governed by reason. For you ought to know that the Lord, who had given this delight, can also give another, better one, and is able to fill the need by some other means. As for benefit, just as you see your own, you ought also to consider that of him who has died: for perhaps it was expedient for him so, as it is written: He was snatched away, lest wickedness should change his understanding. For his soul was pleasing to God; therefore he hastened to lead him out from the midst of iniquity (Wis. 4:11-14). And what shall I say of familiarity? Time makes one forget it so thoroughly that it seems never to have existed. What then time and the passing days achieve, reason and good reflection ought much more to achieve. And this above all must be considered, which the divine sentence has defined through the Apostle, That the sorrow of the world works death (2 Cor. 7:10). And if delight as well as present benefit or familiarity are things of the world and transitory joys of this age, to cast down the soul and sadden the spirit on their account—see that it is not truly a deadly sickness. Repeating it again and again I will say: That the sorrow of the world works death. And why does it work death? Because excessive sorrow usually leads either to doubt or to dangerous blasphemy.

CHAPTER IV. Mourning was permitted to those before Christ. Why Christ wept for Lazarus. But someone will say: Do you forbid mourning the dead, when both the Patriarchs were wept for, and Moses that servant of God, and then many prophets, especially when the most just Job too tore his garment over the death of his sons (Job 1:20)? It is not I who forbid mourning the dead, but the Apostle, the enlightener of the Gentiles, who says thus: I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, that you may not be saddened as those who have no hope (1 Thess. 4:12). The brightness of the Gospel cannot be obscured if those who had been placed before the Law or under the shadow of the Law wept for their dead. And they rightly wept, because Christ had not yet come from heaven, who dried up that fountain of tears by his resurrection. They rightly wept, because the sentence of death still remained. They rightly lamented, because the resurrection was not yet preached. The saints indeed all hoped for the coming of the Lord; but meanwhile they wept for the dead, because they had not yet seen him whom they hoped for. Indeed, Simeon, one of the ancient saints, who had earlier been anxious about his death, after he received in his hands Jesus the Lord, still a child according to the flesh, rejoices at his departure, saying: Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, in peace, for my eyes have seen your salvation (Luke 2:29). O that blessed Simeon! Because he had seen what he hoped for, he now reckoned his death as peace and rest. But you will say: See, in the Gospel we read that the ruler of the synagogue wept for his daughter (ibid. 8:52), and that the sisters of Lazarus wept for Lazarus (John 11:31). But they still thought according to the old law, because they had not yet seen Christ risen from the dead. The Lord himself plainly wept for Lazarus, already buried (ibid. 33), certainly not to give a pattern for weeping over the dead, but to show by his tears that he had taken on a true body. Or surely he wept with human love over the Jews, because even when such a sign had been shown they were not going to believe in him. For the death of Lazarus could not be a cause of tears, since Jesus himself had both said that he was sleeping and promised that he would raise him, as he also did.

CHAPTER V. It is no longer permitted to mourn the dead. Those alive on the day of judgement will not die. So the ancients, who preceded the coming of Christ, had their own custom and their own frailty. But now, since the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, since the last Adam undid the sentence given to the first Adam, since he destroyed our death by his death, and the Lord rose from the underworld on the third day, death is no longer terrible to the faithful: setting is not feared, because the Rising has come from on high. The Lord himself, who cannot lie, cries out: I am, he says, the resurrection and the life: whoever believes in me, even if he has died, shall live; and everyone who lives and believes in me shall not see death for ever (John 11:25, 26). The divine voice is clear, dearest brothers, that whoever believes in Christ and keeps his commandments, if he has died, shall live. The blessed apostle Paul, receiving this voice and holding it with all the strength of faith, taught: I do not want you, he says, to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, that you may not be sad (1 Thess. 4:12). O wonderful utterance of the Apostle! With one word, before he sets out his teaching, he commends the resurrection. For he calls those who have died sleepers, so that in saying they sleep he may mark them without doubt as going to rise. Do not, he says, be sad concerning those who sleep, as the others also are. Let those who have no hope be saddened: but let us, who are children of hope, rejoice together. And what our hope is, he himself relates, saying: If we believe that Christ died and rose again, so also God will bring with him, through Jesus, those who have fallen asleep (ibid. 13). For Jesus is salvation to us while we live here, and life to us as we depart hence. For me, says the Apostle, to live is Christ, and to die is gain (Phil. 1:21). Gain indeed, because a swift death gains [release from] the distresses and tribulations which a longer life holds. Next the Apostle describes the order and form of our hope. This, he says, we tell you by the word of the Lord, that we who live, who are left, shall not at his coming precede those who have fallen asleep: for the Lord himself, at the command and voice of the Archangel and at the trumpet of God, will descend from heaven, and the dead who are in Christ will rise first: then we who live will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord (1 Thess. 4:14-16). This is what he says: that when the Lord comes he will find many Christians in the body who have not yet experienced death; and yet they will not be caught up to heaven before the holy dead have risen from their tombs, roused by the trumpet of God and the voice of the Archangel. And when they have been roused, joined together with the living they will be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so they will reign with him always. Nor indeed can it be doubted that bodies, though heavy, can be lifted into the air, since at the Lord's command Peter too, having this same body, walked upon the waves of the sea (Matt. 14:29); and Elijah also, to confirm this hope, was snatched up through this air to heaven in a fiery chariot (4 Kings 2:11).

CHAPTER VI. What we shall be like after the resurrection. Death is more to be desired than mourned. Yet it is not to be brought upon oneself. But perhaps you ask what those who have risen from the dead will be like. Hear your Lord himself saying: Then, he says, the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father (Matt. 13:43). Why should I speak of the brightness of the sun, when the faithful must be transfigured to the glory of Christ the Lord himself, as the apostle Paul testifies: Our way of life, he says, is in heaven. From there we also await the Saviour himself, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our lowliness into conformity with the body of his glory (Phil. 3:20-21). Without doubt this mortal flesh will be transfigured into conformity with the glory of Christ, and the mortal will put on immortality: for what had been sown in weakness will forthwith rise in power (1 Cor. 15:43). The flesh will no longer fear corruption; it will not suffer hunger, nor thirst, nor sicknesses, nor misfortunes. For there is safe peace and firm security of life. Heavenly glory is indeed of another kind, where joy also will be granted without failing.

Bearing these things in his mind and before his eyes, blessed Paul said: I desired to be dissolved and to be with Christ, which is much better (Phil. 1:23). And further, teaching openly: While we are in the body, he says, we are on pilgrimage away from the Lord; for we walk by faith and not by sight. But we have, he says, rather the good will to be on pilgrimage away from the body and to be present with the Lord (2 Cor. 5:6-8). What are we doing, we men of little faith, who are distressed and lose heart if one of our dear ones departs to the Lord? What are we doing, we whom pilgrimage in this world delights more than being brought into the sight of Christ? Truly, truly, all that we live is a pilgrimage: for like pilgrims in this age we have uncertain dwellings; we toil, we sweat, walking roads that are hard and full of dangers; on every side there are snares from spiritual and from bodily enemies, on every side little paths of error have been laid ready. And though we are pressed by such great dangers, not only do we ourselves not long to be set free, but we even mourn and lament those who have been set free as though they were lost. What has God bestowed on us through his Only-begotten, if we still fear the fall of death? Why do we glory in being reborn of water and the Spirit, we who are saddened by departure from this world? The Lord himself cries out: If anyone serves me, let him follow me; and where I am, there my servant also will be (John 12:26). Do you think that if an earthly king were to call someone to his palace or banquet, he would not hasten there with thanksgiving? How much more must we run to the heavenly King, who will make those whom he receives not only his guests but also his fellow-rulers, as it is written: If we have died with him, we shall also live with him; if we endure, we shall also reign with him (2 Tim. 2:11-12). Nor do I say this so that anyone should lay hands on himself, or kill himself against the will of God the Creator, or drive his soul out of the lodging of his body; but I say this: that glad and rejoicing, when either he himself or his neighbour is called, he should both go himself and congratulate those who go. For this is the sum of the Christian faith: to await true life after death, to hope for return after departure. Having received, then, the word of the Apostle, let us now say with confidence: Thanks be to God, who has given us victory over death through Christ our Lord (1 Cor. 15:57); to whom be glory and power now and for ever and ever. Amen.
Second Sermon.

CHAPTER I. Why the resurrection is doubted among unbelievers. In the preceding little book we touched briefly on consolation in mortality and on the hope of resurrection; now we hasten to speak of the same things more fully and more forcefully. For the things I have said are certain to the faithful, but to unbelievers and doubters they seem to be fables; to them let us set out a few things more concisely. Certainly, whoever of you are unbelieving, all the doubt you hold concerns the substance of the body. For some disbelieve that flesh turned to dust can rise again and live again. But concerning the soul no one can doubt, since even the philosophers themselves, though they are pagans, do not disagree about the immortality of the soul. For what is death but the separation of body and soul? For when the soul departs, which lives always and knows not how to die, since it is from the breath of God, the body alone dies: for one thing in us is mortal, another immortal. But the departing soul, which is not seen by fleshly eyes, is received by Angels and placed either in the bosom of Abraham, if it is faithful, or in the custody of the prison of hell, if it is sinful, until the appointed day comes on which it is to receive back its body and, before the tribunal of Christ the true judge, render an account of its works. Therefore, since all the hesitation is about the flesh, its weakness must be defended and its resurrection affirmed.

CHAPTER II. The sprouting of seeds proves it possible. Creation also proves it. But if anyone, doubtful and unbelieving, asks of me: How will the dead rise? With what body will they come? I will answer him with the mouth and words of the Apostle: Fool, what you sow is not brought to life unless it first dies; and what you sow, you sow as a bare grain of wheat, or of some other seed (1 Cor. 15:36-37), dead and dry, without moisture; and when it has rotted, it rises more fruitfully, and is clothed with husks and armed with awns. He then who raises up a grain of wheat for your sake, who daily raises the sun as if from the tomb of night, and restores the moon as if from its perishing, and calls back the departing seasons, for our benefit of course: will he not seek out us ourselves, for whose sake he restores all things, and will he allow those to be extinguished once for all whom he kindled with his breath, whom he animated with his spirit? And will man, who both acknowledged him piously and worshipped him, exist no more for ever? But do you still doubt that you can be restored after death, reconstituted after ashes and consumed bones? O man, tell me: what were you before you were conceived in your mother's womb? Nothing, certainly. Will not God, then, who created you out of nothing, be able more easily to restore you out of something? Believe me, he who could create what did not exist will more easily be able to remake what already existed before. He who commanded you to grow from a drop of formless fluid in your mother's womb into sinews, veins and bones will be able, believe me, to beget you again from the womb of the earth. But do you fear that perhaps your dry bones cannot be clothed with their former flesh? Do not, do not judge the majesty of God by your own powerlessness. That God, the creator of all things, who clothes trees with leaves and meadows with flowers, will be able also to clothe your bones at once in the resurrection, as in springtime. The prophet Ezekiel once doubted about this very thing, and when asked by the Lord whether the dry bones which were seen scattered over the plain would live, he answered: You know, Lord. But after he saw, at God's command and by his own prophesying, the bones running to their places and joints; after he saw the dry bones bound with sinews, interwoven with veins, covered with flesh, clothed with skin, he afterwards prophesied in the spirit; and the spirit of each one came and entered into those lying bodies, and they rose again and soon stood up. Thus confirmed concerning the resurrection, the Prophet wrote down the vision, so that knowledge of so great a thing might reach posterity (Ezek. 37:3-10). Rightly, then, does Isaiah cry out: The dead will arise, and those who are in the tombs will rise again, and those who are in the earth will rejoice. For the dew that is from you is health to them (Isa. 26:19). For truly, as seeds moistened with dew sprout and spring up, so by the dew of the Spirit the bones of the faithful will sprout.

CHAPTER III. And a huge flame from a small flint. But do you doubt how the whole man can be restored from small bones? Indeed, you raise a huge flame from a small spark of fire; will God not be able, from the small leaven of your ashes, to make whole again the entire dough of your little body? And if you say: Nowhere do the remains of that flesh appear, for perhaps they have been consumed by fire or devoured by beasts, know this first, that whatever is consumed is held in the bowels of the earth, from where it can be brought forth again at God's command. For you too, when no fire is visible, apply a small stone and a little iron, and strike out of the bowels of the stone as much fire as is needed. What, then, you do by your own industry and wisdom, which God himself has granted you, [so as to bring forth what does not appear]: will that divine majesty not be able to do by its own power, [so as to strike out the things which for the meantime are not seen]? Believe me, God can do all things.

CHAPTER IV. That the resurrection will truly come is attested by Christ, the Apostles, the examples of the martyrs, and the mother of the Maccabees. Hence the fear of death is shut out. The command not to mourn. Ask only this: whether he has promised that he will bring about the resurrection. And when you have learned that it was promised, from the testimony of so many, indeed when you hold the most certain pledge of Christ the Lord himself, be strengthened in faith and stop fearing death now. For whoever still fears disbelieves; whoever disbelieves incurs an incurable sin, because by his unbelief he dares to declare God either powerless or, certainly, a liar. But the blessed Apostles do not show it so, nor do the holy martyrs. The Apostles, for the sake of this preaching of the resurrection, preaching that Christ had risen and announcing that in him the dead will be raised, refused neither death, nor torments, nor crosses. If, then, every word stands on the mouth of two or three witnesses, how can the resurrection of the dead be called into doubt, when so many and such fit witnesses exist for it, who bear testimony to it with the shedding of their blood? And what of the holy martyrs? Did they have a sure hope of resurrection, or not? If they had not had it, they would certainly not have undergone death through such great tortures and punishments as the greatest gain: they did not think of the present tortures, but of the rewards to follow. They knew the saying: The things that are seen are for a time; but the things that are not seen are eternal (2 Cor. 4:18). Hear, brothers, an example of courage. A mother was urging on her seven sons, and did not mourn, but rather rejoiced. She saw her sons scraped with hooks, cut to pieces with iron, roasted in a frying pan; and she shed no tears, raised no wailing, but anxiously urged her sons to endurance. For she was certainly not cruel, but faithful: she loved her sons, not softly, but bravely. She urged her sons on to the suffering which she too joyfully underwent. For she was secure about her own resurrection and that of her sons (2 Macc. 7). Why should I speak of men, of women, of boys, of girls? How they made sport of this death, how with the greatest speed they passed over to the heavenly army! They certainly could have lived for the present, had they wished, since it was in their own power to live by denying Christ or to die by confessing him; but they chose rather to throw away the temporary life and take up the everlasting life, to be shut out from the earth and to dwell in heaven.

Amid all this, brothers, what room is there for doubt? Where can the fear of death still remain? If we are sons of the martyrs, if we wish to be found their companions, let us not be saddened by death, let us not mourn our dear ones who go before us to the Lord. For if we choose to lament, the blessed martyrs themselves will mock us and say: O faithful, O you who desire the kingdom of God, you who lament and mourn with grief your dear ones who die softly, in beds, indeed, and on feathers: if you saw them tortured and killed by the Gentiles for the name of the Lord, what would you do? Or has no example gone before you? The patriarch Abraham, offering his only son as a sacrifice, slew him with the sword of obedience (Gen. 22:10); nor did he spare him whom he loved with so great a love, so that he might be proved obedient to the Lord. But if you say that he did this because of God's command, you too have a command, that you should not be sad about those who sleep (1 Thess. 4:12). Those, then, who do not keep the least things, when will they keep the greater? Or do you not know that a mind which breaks in such matters is found worthless for stronger things? Who that fears a stream ever enters the sea? So whoever laments impatiently one he has lost, when will he be able to reach the contest of martyrdom? For whoever stands firm and great-souled in these things already lays down for himself a step towards greater ones.

CHAPTER V. A distinguished example of this from David. Therefore it is not permitted to wear black garments for mourning. The answer of a heathen on hearing of his son's death. Heathens, Jews and catechumens who die are to be lamented. Which sorrow is salutary. Summary of both sermons. Let these things suffice, brothers, for contempt of death and for the strengthening of the hope to come. It remains for me to bring forward one example from the ancients, which may provide every consolation, and which I want all to hear with the patient ears of the heart. David, the great king, bore most impatiently that his beloved son, whom he loved as his own soul, was struck with sickness; and when human aid was no longer of any use, he turned himself to the Lord. Laying aside royal glory, he sat on the ground, lay in sackcloth, did not eat, did not drink, praying to God for seven days on end, in case perhaps his son might be granted to him. The elders of his house came and, consoling him, begged him to take bread, fearing that perhaps, while he wished his son to live, he himself might die first. They could not wring it from him, nor force him; for impatient love is wont to scorn dangers themselves. The king lies in the squalor of sackcloth while his son is sick: neither do words bring consolation, nor does the very need for food call him. His mind feeds on sorrow, his breast is refreshed with grief, his eyes flow with tears in place of drink. Meanwhile what God had decreed came to pass. The boy dies. The wife in mourning, the whole house in lamentation, the servants fearful, anxiously wondering what would happen: for no one dared announce to their master that his son was dead, fearing, of course, that he who so impatiently mourned him while still alive might, on hearing he was dead, put an end to his own life. While the servants murmur among themselves, while in sadness one urges another to speak or forbids it, David understood; he forestalls the messengers and asks whether his son has breathed out his life. They cannot deny it; they show by their weeping what has happened. There is an unusual gathering, great suspense and fear lest the devoted father should bring some harm upon himself. At once King David rises from the sackcloth, rises cheerful, as if he had heard that his son was safe: he goes to the baths, washes his body, goes to the temple, worships God, feasts with his friends, his sighs suppressed, all groaning laid aside, his face now glad. The household marvel, his friends are astonished at this new and sudden change of conduct; at last they dare to ask what he meant by this, that while his son was alive he grieved so, and now that he was dead he did not grieve. That man, outstanding in greatness of soul, answered: It was necessary, while my son was still living, both to humble myself and to fast and to mourn in the sight of the Lord, for there was hope of obtaining an extension of his life; but now that the will of the Lord has been done, it is foolish and impious to wear the mind away with useless lamentation. So saying: I shall go to him, he will not return to me (2 Kgs. 12:16-23). Here is an example of greatness of soul and courage. But if that David, still placed under the law, under, I do not say the licence, but the necessity of lamentation, so separated his mind from irrational mourning, so checked his own sorrow and that of his household: we who are now under grace, under the sure hope of resurrection, to whom all sorrow is forbidden, with what face do we lament our dead after the manner of the Gentiles, raise mad wailings like revellers of another kind, tear our tunics and bare our breasts, and sing empty words and dirges around the body and tomb of the departed? Finally, for what reason do we dye our garments black, unless to prove ourselves truly faithless and wretched, not only by our weeping but also by our clothing? These things are foreign, brothers, they are alien, they are not permitted; and even if they were permitted, they would not be fitting. But some of the brothers and sisters, though their own faith and the Lord's command make them strong, are nevertheless weakened and broken by the opinion of relatives and neighbours, lest they be judged stony and cruel if they spare their clothing, if they do not rave in frenzied mourning. And how vain, how foolish this is, to consider the opinions of erring men, and not to fear doing something short of the faith one has received! Why does not the one who is like that rather learn endurance, why does not the one who is doubtful learn faith from me? Since, even if the grief of such a heart is great, one ought to digest mourning silently within, and not publish it through the lightness of one's mind.

I want to put forward one more example to correct those who think the dead should be lamented. The example is from the history of the pagans. There was a certain pagan ruler who had an only son, and much loved. While he was sacrificing to his idols on the Capitol in heathen error, it was announced to him that this only son had died. He did not leave the rites he had in hand, he did not weep, he did not sigh at all; but hear what he answered. Let him be buried, he said, for I remember that I begot a mortal son. See the answer, see the courage of a pagan man: he did not even order that he be waited for, or that his son be committed to burial in his presence. What shall we do, brothers, if the devil brings him forward against us before Christ on the day of judgement and says: This worshipper of groves, whom I deceived with my tricks into serving blind and deaf images, to whom I promised neither resurrection from the dead, nor paradise, nor the kingdoms of heaven, this wise man neither grieved nor groaned at the death of his noble and only son, nor at such news abandoned my rites; but your Christians, your faithful, for whom you were crucified and died precisely so that they should not fear death but be secure about the resurrection, not only mourn the dead both with voice and dress, but are even ashamed to come forth to church; some even of your clergy and pastors break off their ministry, giving themselves to mourning, as though mocking your will? Why? Because you called those whom you wished out of the darkness of the world to yourself. What shall we be able to answer to this, brothers? Will not confusion seize us, when in this respect we are found inferior to the Gentiles? And indeed the pagan ought to be mourned, who, not knowing God, goes straight to punishment as soon as he dies. The Jew ought to be lamented, who, not believing in Christ, has consigned his soul to perdition. We must clearly grieve over our catechumens, if, through their own unbelief or the negligence of those close to them, they have departed without saving baptism. But whoever, sanctified by grace, sealed by faith, proved by his way of life, or secure in innocence, departs from this world, is to be called blessed, not mourned; longed for, not lamented; but longed for with moderation, since we know that we ourselves will follow as time goes on.

Wipe away your tears, then, break off your sighs, restrain your groans, O believer; and in place of this sorrow put on that saving sorrow which the blessed Apostle said is according to God, which is wont to work a stable salvation (2 Cor. 7:10): namely, repentance for crimes committed. Search your heart, questioning your own conscience, and if you find anything to repent of (and you will find it, since you are human), draw sighs in confession, pour out tears in prayer, be anxious about that true death, about the punishment of the soul; be anxious about sin, as David says: For I declare my iniquity, and I will be anxious for my sin (Ps. 37:19); and you will not be terrified at the temporal dissolution of this body, which in its own time, at God's command, will be restored for the better. See how the divine saying has embraced both, saying: The hour is coming when the dead who are in the tombs will rise. Here is security, here is contempt of death. But what follows? Those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; but those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgement (John 5:28, 29): here is the difference among those who rise. All flesh, that is, all human flesh, must indeed rise; but the good will rise to life, the wicked will rise to punishment, as it is written: Therefore the ungodly will not rise in judgement, nor sinners in the council of the just (Ps. 1:5). So that we may not rise to judgement, then, let us set aside the sorrow of death and take up that repentance and sorrow, and let us take care for good works and a better life; and let the thought of this funeral and this corpse serve us to this end, that we may know that we are mortal, and through this thought may by no means neglect our salvation while there is time, while it is permitted: namely, either bearing fruit for the better, or amending ourselves if we have erred in ignorance; lest, suddenly overtaken by the day of death, we seek a space for repentance and cannot find it; we seek to give alms and make satisfaction for our offences, and what we want is not granted.

Having shown, then, brothers, [the law] of common death, having shown the prohibition of tears, having pointed out the frailty of the ancients and not the strength of Christianity, having pointed out the Lord's mystery and the Apostles' teaching on the resurrection, having recalled the acts of the Apostles and the sufferings of the martyrs, having shown besides the example of David and moreover the deed of a Gentile man, and having finally set out both the harmful and the useful sorrow, the one that harms, the other that saves through repentance: all these things having been shown thus, what else ought we now to do, brothers, but give thanks to God the Father and say, Your will be done as in heaven so on earth (Matt. 6:10): you gave life, you appointed death; you bring into the world, you lead out of the world, and when you have led out, you keep safe; for nothing of yours perishes, since you said that not a hair of their head would perish (Luke 21:18). For you will take away their spirit, and they will fail, and return to their earth; but you will send forth your Spirit and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth (Ps. 103:29, 30)? These words, brothers, are worthy of the faithful, this is saving medicine: the eye wiped with this sponge of consolation, bathed with this eye-salve of reason, will not only not feel the blindness of despair, but will not suffer even any bleariness of sorrow; rather, looking on all things as bright with the eyes of the heart, it will say, after that most patient Job, The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has been done: blessed be the name of the Lord (Job 1:21) for ever and ever. Amen.
PREFATORY NOTE TO THE TREATISE ON THE RIGHTNESS OF CATHOLIC CONDUCT.

This treatise is found in the second book of the Life of St Eligius, bishop of Noyon, chapter 15, collected, no doubt, and written down by the labour of Audoenus, author of that Life, who sought to gather into this sermon the daily and principal admonitions of the most pious prelate to his people. For every day, says Audoenus, he tirelessly exhorted the people entrusted to him with saving admonitions, and, the crowds having gathered to the church from all sides, he would raise his voice with prophetic confidence and deliver to them admonitions of this kind, embracing many great things briefly in his sermon but abundant spiritually for edification: I ask you, dearest brothers, and with great humility I admonish you, etc. Audoenus there presents the whole sermon, and when it is finished he adds: Let it suffice to have related thus far in summary these things from the familiar admonitions of so great a man; and although he did not run through them in order, as they are arranged here, within the span of a single day, yet at various times he always impressed precepts of this kind upon the people. Our old Germanensis codex agrees, which presents this same treatise written separately from the Life of Eligius, with this title: Here begin the sermons of blessed Eligius, which he delivered to the people with the greatest zeal from the richest treasury of his heart. Yet what Eligius sets forth there he drew almost entirely from the Caesarian Sermons, which, through the care of Caesarius (as we have observed elsewhere), were read in the churches throughout all Gaul and through the Spains. Go to the Appendix of the preceding volume, and compare sermons 29, 78, 110, 116, 141, 210, 249, 258, 265, 266, 273, 275, 277, 278, 279, 289, etc. In them you will find both the very words of Eligius and certain passages explained more plainly than here. From Sermon 129, no. 2, for example, and from 130, nos. 1 and 2, you will understand what we read here in no. 5, Let no one make 'little old women' (vetulas): where Jacques Sirmond, just as in the Council of Auxerre, thought that vitulas ['calves'] should be written. Likewise this saying of Eligius in no. 9, He who presumes to have a concubine before lawful marriage sins worse than he who commits adultery, is to be taken in such a way that he is judged to sin worse for no other reason than that his deed sets a more pernicious example; you will learn this from sermon 288, no. 5, of the same Appendix, and from 289, no. 4, where Caesarius gives this reason for that saying: Because he who commits adultery still wishes to do so grave an evil secretly, but he who wishes to have a concubine publicly thinks he may freely commit an execrable thing in full view of the whole people. Thus, indeed, he gives others occasion to go astray, so that they believe it permitted with impunity. For sins, as Augustine says in the Enchiridion, chapter 80, however great and horrible, when they have become habitual, are believed to be either small or none at all.
